Core concepts

Error handling

Route errors into 4-argument middleware, throw HttpError, and understand the default JSON error and 404/405 responses.

next(err) is the switch#

Handlers either finish the response or call next(). Calling next(err) with a truthy value switches the stack into error mode: from that point, only 4-argument error handlers are eligible.

js
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res, next) => {
  const user = users.get(req.params.id);
  if (!user) return next(new HttpError(404, 'user not found'));
  res.json(user);
});

Two things reach error middleware automatically, with no wrapper library:

  • A synchronous throw inside any handler.
  • A rejected promise returned by any handler. The router calls .catch(next) on every returned promise.
js
app.get('/data', async (req, res) => {
  const row = await db.get(req.params.id); // rejection → error middleware
  res.json(row);
});

Express 4 only forwarded synchronous throws; routiva forwards both.

Error middleware#

An error handler is any function whose length === 4. There is no registration API — arity is the marker.

js
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(err.status || 500).json({ error: { message: err.message } });
});

The dispatch loop skips 4-arity functions during normal flow and skips 3-arity functions during error flow, so the same stack serves both.

Ordering matters, exactly as with regular middleware:

  • Register error handlers after the routes whose errors they should catch.
  • Registering one before a route means that route's errors will not reach it, because the cursor has already moved past it.

Inside an error handler you can:

  • Send a response, ending the chain.
  • Call next(err) to pass the error to the next error handler (for example WARN, then a final JSON handler).
  • Call next() with no argument to drop back into normal flow at the current cursor.
  • Call next after the response is sent — the response is write-once, so extra calls are ignored.

HttpError#

HttpError carries an HTTP status and marks itself safe to expose:

js
import { HttpError } from 'routiva';

throw new HttpError(422, 'validation failed', { type: 'validation.failed' });
ArgumentTypeNotes
statusnumberAlso assigned to statusCode
messagestringDefaults to the status reason phrase
options.exposebooleanOverrides the default exposure of the message
options.typestringMachine-readable error code, echoed in the response
options.causeErrorUnderlying error, kept off the wire

error.expose is set to status < 500 || options.expose === true. In other words, 4xx messages are safe to send and 5xx messages are hidden unless you opt in. The constructor also preserves a cause and sets the error name to HttpError.

Convenience constructors:

CallStatus
HttpError.badRequest(message?, options?)400
HttpError.unauthorized(message?, options?)401
HttpError.forbidden(message?, options?)403
HttpError.notFound(message?, options?)404
HttpError.methodNotAllowed(message?, options?)405
HttpError.tooLarge(message?, options?)413
HttpError.internal(message?, options?)500

The default error handler#

If no error middleware sends a response, App._handleError runs. It normalises the error first: it accepts anything (next('oops') becomes new Error('oops')), reads err.status or err.statusCode, and uses it only when it is an integer between 400 and 599. Everything else becomes 500.

The body is JSON:

json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "user not found",
    "status": 404,
    "type": "validation.failed"
  }
}
  • type is included only when error.type is set.
  • stack is included only when the expose stack setting is on and the status is >= 500 and a stack exists.
  • message is error.message when the error is exposed or expose stack is on; otherwise it is the canonical reason phrase for the status.

expose stack and production#

The expose stack setting defaults to env !== 'production', where env comes from options.env, then NODE_ENV, then 'development'. So in development the real message and a 5xx stack are returned; with NODE_ENV=production a 500 returns { "error": { "message": "Internal Server Error", "status": 500 } } with no stack.

ErrorexposeDevelopmentProduction
HttpError(404, 'user not found')trueuser not founduser not found
HttpError(500, 'db down')falsedb down + stackInternal Server Error
new Error('boom')unsetboom + stackInternal Server Error

Set it explicitly with app.set('expose stack', true/false) or the exposeStack constructor option. For a single error, set options.expose: true on the HttpError.

Headers already sent#

If a handler throws after it has started writing, the response cannot be replaced. The default handler checks res.raw.headersSent and, rather than crashing with ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT, aborts the socket with res.raw.destroy(). Your own error middleware should make the same check:

js
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.raw.headersSent) return next(err); // let the default handler abort
  res.status(500).json({ error: { message: 'Internal Server Error', status: 500 } });
});

404, 405 and OPTIONS#

When the stack is exhausted without an error, _handleNotFound runs. If any route matched the path but not the method, that method is recorded and the response describes what is allowed.

SituationResponse
No path matched404 + { error: { message: 'Not Found', status: 404, path: req.originalUrl } }
Path matched, wrong method405 + Allow header + { error: { message: 'Method Not Allowed', status: 405 } }
OPTIONS on a known path204 + Allow header, empty body

The Allow list is sorted and always includes OPTIONS. When a GET route exists, HEAD is recorded alongside it, so a GET-only path reports Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. This is stricter than Express, which returns 404 for a wrong method, and matches RFC 9110.

Customising#

Add your own error middleware after the routes. A typical handler logs, then renders a stable shape:

js
import { App, HttpError } from 'routiva';

const app = new App();

app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => {
  throw new HttpError(404, 'user not found', { type: 'user.not_found' });
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.raw.headersSent) return next(err);
  const status = err.status || err.statusCode || 500;
  res.status(status).json({
    error: {
      message: status < 500 ? err.message : 'internal error',
      status,
      type: err.type,
    },
  });
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  // Fallback: delegate anything unhandled to the built-in handler.
  next(err);
});

To replace the default 404 itself, register a terminal middleware or catch-all route after your real routes; it will run before _handleNotFound gets a chance:

js
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: { message: 'Not Found', status: 404, path: req.originalUrl } });
});
